description: Three engineering students from Euromed University of Fes. One question every Moroccan farmer asks each autumn: what do I plant this year? We are Astravia: Hajar Belghali (team leader, cybersecurity), Chaimae Ouarab (software engineering) and Houda Fettouh (cybersecurity). We built SAMA (سما, “sky”) to turn forty years of NASA data into a voice farmers can follow, in Darija, Arabic, French and English. Honest by design. Rooted in Moroccan fields.
summary:
SAMA (سما, “sky”) is a mobile decision-support app for Moroccan farmers. It answers four questions: what to plant, how much water it needs, when to act, and what risk to watch. Farmers often decide before they know how the season will turn out, and the NASA data that could help is in English, in technical tables. SAMA turns 40 years of NASA POWER data (1984–2024) into one clear answer: for example, “this crop gave a good season in 3 of the last 4 years here.”
It uses FAO-56 and FAO-33 agronomic formulas and replays 1,000 possible futures built from real past seasons. It is not machine learning and not a weather forecast, and every result says so. The app works in Darija, Arabic, French and English, with a simple farmer mode and an adviser mode with the numbers. A “Why this advice?” screen shows the 40 real seasons behind each answer. This helps farmers adapt to a changing climate and use scarce water better.
details:
WHAT IT DOES:

SAMA (سما, "sky") is a mobile decision-support app for small farmers in Morocco. It answers four questions: what to plant, how much water to plan for, when to act, and what risk to watch. It turns 40 years of NASA POWER data (1984–2024) into a clear answer, such as "this crop gave a good season in X years out of 10", and shows the real seasons behind it. Starting areas: the Saïs plain (Meknès), Erfoud and other regional points, 15 locations in total.

HOW IT WORKS:

1. Data: NASA POWER daily rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation, 1984–2024, bundled in the app for 15 locations. The data was audited against a fresh NASA download (no differences, no missing days).

2. Water need: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0). Crop need: ETc = Kc × ET0.

3. Soil water: a daily soil-water balance, rainfed by default, with optional irrigation.

4. Yield: FAO-33 relative yield, 1 − Ky × (1 − ETa/ETc). A season counts as good if yield reaches 80% (adjustable).

5. Futures: a Monte-Carlo simulation builds 1,000 three-season futures from whole real past seasons (fixed seed, so results are reproducible). Results read "X in 10", meaning all three seasons were good.

This is not machine learning and not a weather forecast.

FEATURES:

- Farmer mode (simple, big buttons, crop photos) and Adviser mode (numbers, several farms, editable assumptions).

- 32 crops with a status: explore, use caution, or more information needed. 7 crops without a documented FAO-33 value are shown with "?" and are never recommended.

- Time Machine: three seasons in a row with rotation scenarios.

- Climate Shock Lab: "what if it rains less?" (−20%, −40%) and +2 °C, always labelled as a scenario, not an observation.

- Detective: asks one question, only when the answer changes the result.

- Satellite Lens: NASA GIBS layers with their resolution stated, and a simple place comparison (season rain minus ET0).

- "Why this advice?": the 40 real seasons, sources and assumptions.

- Four languages: Darija, Arabic, French and English (328 text entries).

- Location by GPS, search or map, with a privacy screen. If exact data is missing, the app uses the nearest reference, shows the distance and asks for confirmation.

WHAT WORKS TODAY, AND WHAT IT STILL NEEDS:

- Tested: 112 automated tests and static analysis pass. The app has been run in Chrome and on a phone by the team.

- Voice: the app has a voice-search bar, speaker buttons and a voice-command assistant with a closed vocabulary in four languages. Audio playback is designed to use pre-generated clips. These clips have not been generated yet, so the app falls back to showing the text. Planned: generate Darija clips with the public SpeechT5 Darija model (HAMMALE). Speech recognition has not been tested across devices.

- Offline: works offline for the 15 bundled locations. A new location needs an internet connection once, to download its NASA data.

- Satellite Lens: the layer information and place comparison work. The map background needs a map-tile provider, which is not configured yet, so the map shows pins on a blank background.

- Crop parameters (Kc, Ky) are marked "provisional, to be verified" against the FAO tables.

- NASA rainfall has not yet been compared with local rain-gauge data.

- Darija and Arabic text are drafts awaiting native-speaker review.

- The model is simple: no growing roots, no direct temperature effect on yield, seasons assumed independent.

- Not yet tested with farmers in the field.

HONESTY:

Not a forecast and not a guarantee. NASA data is a grid cell (about 50 km), not a field sensor, and satellite rain can differ from rain gauges. Scenarios are always labelled. Every result says "based on 40 past seasons of NASA data".

TOOLS:

Flutter/Dart; Python scripts for NASA data download and audit; flutter_map; NASA POWER and NASA GIBS.

IMPACT (INTENDED):

Fewer lost seasons and better use of scarce water, with advice a farmer or adviser can check. Not yet measured.

IMAGE NOTE:

The 32 crop photos were collected from public web sources. Their owners and licences are not yet verified. They are used for illustration in this competition prototype only, and we will replace them with credited free-licence images before any release.

AI USE:

The code was mostly written with Claude Code (Anthropic), directed, tested and reviewed by the team. Slide images were generated with Canva AI and carry a visible "AI-generated image" mark. Text drafts, including translations, were written with AI assistance and need native-speaker review. The Darija voice feature is designed to use the public SpeechT5 Darija model by HAMMALE. Planning, scientific choices and review were done by the team.
